newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Army mulling enclosing Ft. Bragg.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Army mulling enclosing Ft. Bragg.

text.p: Citing the threat of domestic terrorism in light of the Oklahoma City bombing, officials at the U.S. Army's Fort Bragg said Monday they were mulling closing off the sprawling base with 100 miles (161 km) of gates and fences.
The project would take years and cost $5-6 million for materials and labour alone, according to commercial fence suppliers with experience erecting military security fencing.
But it is a worthwhile project, said Major Jerry O'Hara, spokesman for the Army's 18th Airborne Corps at Fort Bragg, the largest U.S. Army base with more than 40,000 soldiers.
"There have been discussions for years about limiting access to Fort Bragg, but those discussions became sharply focused after the Oklahoma City bombing two years ago," he said.
The bombing of Oklahoma City's Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killed 168 people, the deadliest such attack on civilians ever on U.S. soil.
Lieut. Gen. Jack Keane, Fort Bragg's commander, has submitted his request for approval and funding to Forces Command in Atlanta.

Base officials said the fencing would not mean the public would not be able to drive on Fort Bragg, visit its museums and attend open-house events at the base, which is also home to the 82nd Airborne Division.
Army officials at the Pentagon in Washington said the proposal involved Fort Bragg only and did not signal any larger move to fence in domestic military bases.
